newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sends troops to clear gold mine squatters.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sends troops to clear gold mine squatters.

text.p: The Brazilian government sent in troops and federal police on Thursday to clear wildcat gold-diggers from a huge gold deposit in the Amazon, a Justice Ministry spokeswoman said.

A spokeswoman for state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), which owns the mine, said she believed the operation had passed peacefully and had been directed at removing militants blocking a road to the gold field.
"As far as we know, the operation was carried out without incident, without violence," she said by telephone from the town of Carajas, in the northern state of Para.
The Justice Ministry spokeswoman said the operation at the Serra Leste mine, near Serra Pelada, site of the largest gold rush in history, began at 5 a.m. (0700 GMT).
"We can give no further details for security reasons," she said.
Hundreds of "garimpeiros", as freelance gold prospectors are called in Portuguese, have succeeded in blocking survey work at Serra Leste since May, causing CVRD up to $10 million in losses.
The deposit is thought to contain about 150 tonnes of the precious metal, buried deep beneath the soil.

The garimpeiros claim a share of the profits because it lies near the Serra Pelada gold mine, where at their peak in 1988, up to one million freelancers produced 90 tonnes out of Brazil's total gold production of 113 tonnes.

Serra Pelada was made famous throughout the world by the "human anthill" images of Brazilian photographer Sebastiao Salgado, showing thousands of garimpeiros lugging baskets of rocks up precarious ladders.
Once the world's largest opencast mine, Serra Pelada is now a memorial to those who died in the malaria-infested jungle, chasing dreams of overnight fortunes.
The discovery in February of another massive deposit of gold at nearby Serra Leste revived their dreams of becoming rich.
Jose Antonio Machado, head of the garimpeiros labour union, wrote in Thursday's Correio Braziliense newspaper that the cost of sending in the army to clear out the squatters would be high.

Taking a jibe at the social-democrat credentials of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, a sociology professor turned head of government, Machado said Cardoso would never have used the armed forces against helpless miners in the past.
"When he was still a presidential candidate, he would never have taken by force this filthy gold mine, whose exploration will cost even more if tainted with injuries," he said.
A court has ruled against the freelancers' claim to the gold in Serra Leste, paving the way for the military operation.

The CVRD spokeswoman in Carajas said the aim was to remove a group of about 50 militants blocking the road into Serra Leste. The protesters had managed to stop surveys by threatening workers and blocking cars and trucks from entering.
